title: Two Stories about Flying
summary: This chapter pairs two tales of flight. In 'His First Flight' by Liam O'Flaherty, a young seagull, paralysed by the fear that his wings will not support him, watches his family fly away and starves alone on his ledge until his mother's trick with a piece of fish tempts him to dive; his wings spread by instinct, fear gives way to joy, and he lands safely on the green sea. In 'The Black Aeroplane' by Frederick Forsyth, a pilot flying his old Dakota home to England for breakfast enters a storm cloud, loses his compass, radio and instruments, and is saved by a mysterious black aeroplane whose pilot waves him on; he lands safely, but the control room woman says no other plane was seen on radar, leaving the help a haunting mystery.
hotTopics: Fear of flying and the young seagull's hesitation
The mother's trick with the piece of fish
The first flight and landing on the green sea
Courage comes when fear is faced
The Dakota flight to England for breakfast
Failure of compass, radio and instruments
The mysterious black aeroplane that guided the pilot
No other aeroplane on the radar
Nature versus fear in both stories

sections.heading: About the Authors
sections.para: The two stories come from two very different writers. Liam O'Flaherty (1896-1984) was an Irish novelist and short story writer famous for his keen observation of animals and birds in their natural surroundings; stories like 'His First Flight' show his love of nature and his belief that behaviour in the animal world mirrors human life. Frederick Forsyth (1938-) is a British novelist and journalist, celebrated for thrillers such as 'The Day of the Jackal'; he was himself a pilot in the Royal Air Force, which gives 'The Black Aeroplane' its authentic aviation detail. Together the two stories balance each other: one is a naturalist's study of a bird learning courage, the other a flier's tale of an inexplicable rescue in the sky, and both ask what happens when a creature is forced to act beyond its fear.
points: Liam O'Flaherty was an Irish writer known for stories about animals and the wild beauty of nature.
In 'His First Flight' he studies a bird's psychology with the precision of a naturalist.
Frederick Forsyth is a British thriller writer who served as a pilot in the Royal Air Force.
His flying experience lends realism to the cockpit details of 'The Black Aeroplane'.
Both stories place a flyer at a moment of crisis and test his courage.
One story ends in natural explanation, the other in an unsolved mystery.

keyTerms.meaning: A writer or scientist who studies animals and plants in nature.
A narrow rock shelf where the young seagull stood alone.
The compartment where a pilot sits and controls an aeroplane.
Something unexplained, like the black aeroplane of the second story.

sections.trick: O'Flaherty observes, Forsyth flies: an Irish naturalist writes about wings in nature, a British pilot writes about wings in a storm.
sections.examPointer: One markers may ask the author of either story; keep both names paired with their nationalities and professions.

sections.heading: His First Flight: The Seagull's Fear
sections.para: The young seagull was alone on his ledge, for his two brothers and his sister had already flown away the day before. Though his wings were as long as theirs, he had not the courage to make his first flight, because he felt certain that his wings would never support him, and the great expanse of sea stretched down beneath him, miles down. His parents had taught his brothers and sister to skim the waves and dive for fish, and they flew about perfecting their aerobatics while he stood looking at them. When he ran back to the little hole under the ledge where he slept at night, his father and mother came around calling to him shrilly, upbraiding him and threatening to let him starve on his ledge unless he flew away. Yet not one harsh word could move him to fly, for his fear was stronger than his hunger.
points: The young seagull's two brothers and sister had flown away, leaving him alone on the ledge.
Despite having wings as long as theirs, he feared they would never support him.
The sea lay miles below, and the drop terrified him more than hunger did.
His parents had taught the others to skim the waves and to dive for fish.
The family taunted him and threatened to let him starve on his ledge unless he flew.
For twenty-four hours he ate nothing, watching his family enjoy their food.

keyTerms.meaning: To scold or reproach someone sharply.
To mock or jeer at a person's weakness.
To move lightly just above a surface, as the gulls skimmed the waves.
Impressive flying manoeuvres, like dips and rises in the air.

sections.trick: Wings ready, courage missing: the seagull's problem is not feathers but fear, and fear grows while hunger waits.
sections.examPointer: Questions ask why the young seagull was afraid and how his family treated him; quote the line about wings that would never support him.

sections.heading: The Mother's Trick and the First Flight
sections.para: The next morning the mother seagull found the solution. She took a piece of fish and flew across to him with it, almost within reach of his beak; he waited a moment, surprised and joyful, then dived at the fish with a loud scream. His mother flew upward and halted just out of reach, and as he swooped helplessly after her, his wings spread outwards, the wind rushed against them, and he realised he was flying. The next moment he was soaring upward, terror gone, calling happily to his mother. His brothers and sister came curveting and banking and soaring and diving around him, and after that first triumph he flew out over the green sea, finally landing on its surface, where his legs sank into the water and his belly touched it, and he was too frightened to fly for a moment; but he floated safely, for seagulls are made for the sea as much as the sky.
points: The mother seagull tempted her young one with a piece of fish, flying just out of his reach.
Driven by hunger, he dived at the fish and fell outward and downward into space.
At the critical moment his wings spread outwards and cut through the air, and his fear vanished.
He soared upward with joy, and his siblings flew around him curveting, banking and diving.
He landed on the green sea, first with his legs sinking in, then floated safely on its surface.
The first flight was won not by force but by temptation, instinct and necessity working together.

keyTerms.meaning: To dive or throw oneself suddenly downward.
To descend swiftly through the air.
To rest on the surface of water without sinking.
Inborn behaviour, like the automatic spreading of the wings.

sections.trick: FISH frees fear: a Fish In Sight, Hunger wins, courage appears and wings remember their work.
sections.examPointer: The mother's trick is a favourite short question; describe the sequence dive, fall, spread, soar in the same order for full marks.

sections.heading: His First Flight: Courage and the Theme
sections.para: O'Flaherty's story is a lesson in how courage is born. The young seagull's body was ready, for his wings were as long as his family's, but his mind held him captive; fear, not weakness, kept him starving on the ledge. The parents' harsh strategy of taunts and threats fails, and it is the mother's clever temptation that succeeds, showing that encouragement works better than scolding. Once the first step is taken, fear evaporates and joy takes its place, and what seemed impossible becomes natural. The story therefore carries a universal message: we must overcome our hesitation and take the first step, because wings that seem useless are ready to work the moment we trust them. It also mirrors human families, where youngsters delay leaving the safety of home until necessity and gentle challenge push them into the world.
points: Fear, not physical weakness, is the true obstacle to the young seagull's flight.
Harsh taunts from the family fail, but the mother's temptation succeeds, proving encouragement works better.
Hunger is the necessity that forces the crucial dive at the fish.
Courage appears the instant the wings are trusted, and fear turns to joy.
The story mirrors human children who must finally leave the safety of home.
The theme: the first step is the hardest; take it and the rest follows.

keyTerms.meaning: The willingness to act despite fear.
Delay caused by doubt or uncertainty.
Support that gives someone confidence to act.
An important first achievement, like the first flight.

sections.trick: STEP formula: Scared, Tempted, Encounter air, Practice follows; one step turns fear into flight.
sections.examPointer: Theme questions ask what the story teaches; answer that fear must be faced to be conquered, and that the first flight is a symbol of growing up.

sections.heading: The Black Aeroplane: Into the Storm
sections.para: In 'The Black Aeroplane', the narrator, a pilot, is flying his old Dakota aeroplane DS 088 home from Paris to England, dreaming of the holiday ahead and of a big breakfast with his family. Paris control instructs him to turn twelve degrees west, and he is about one hundred and fifty kilometres from Paris when he looks ahead and sees huge black storm clouds. He faces the choice of going back to Paris or flying into the storm, and since he is safely inside the clouds of his own dream of home, he decides to go through them. Inside everything is black: nothing can be seen outside the aeroplane windows, the plane jumps and twists in the air, and then the disaster deepens. The compass and the other instruments stop working, the radio becomes dead, and he realises he has fuel for only five or ten minutes more of flying.
points: The narrator flies an old Dakota DS 088 from Paris to England, longing for breakfast with his family.
Paris control instructs him to turn twelve degrees west, and he is 150 kilometres from Paris.
He sees huge storm clouds and decides to fly into them instead of returning to Paris.
Inside the clouds everything is black, and the old aeroplane jumps and twists in the air.
The compass and other instruments stop working and the radio goes dead.
With fuel sufficient for only five to ten minutes, he is in real danger.

keyTerms.meaning: The instrument that shows direction, which stops working in the storm.
The petrol or gas that powers the plane, almost exhausted.
The ground station that guides aircraft by radio.
Dark towering clouds, called mountains of clouds in the story.

sections.trick: 12 degrees west, 150 km out, 5-10 minutes of fuel: three numbers that mark the pilot's danger.
sections.examPointer: Learn the numbers of this story, the aircraft code, the degrees of turn and the minutes of fuel, as MCQs test them precisely.

sections.heading: The Black Aeroplane: The Mysterious Rescue
sections.para: Just when the narrator believes he is lost, he sees another aeroplane flying through the storm beside him, without lights yet clearly visible, and its pilot waves to him, mouthing to follow. The narrator obeys gladly, turning towards the stranger and following him like an obedient child. The mysterious plane guides him through the darkness, descending until the narrator suddenly emerges beneath the clouds and sees the runway lights below. He lands safely, turns to look for his rescuer, and finds only empty sky. At the control room a woman in the tower tells him calmly that no other aeroplane was seen on the radar that night. The story ends without explanation, leaving the reader to wonder whether the pilot was hallucinating, whether some supernatural force helped him, or whether the black aeroplane was a guardian angel of the skies.
points: A strange aeroplane with no lights appears beside the narrator inside the storm.
Its pilot waves and mouths the words 'Follow me', and the narrator turns to obey.
Guided by the stranger, the narrator descends and breaks out of the clouds to see the runway.
He lands safely with nearly empty fuel tanks and turns to thank the other pilot, but the sky is empty.
The woman in the control centre says his plane was the only one on the radar.
The rescue remains a mystery, suggesting courage, faith or a supernatural helper.

keyTerms.meaning: The electronic system that detects aircraft; it showed no other plane.
The strip on which aircraft land and take off.
The black, unlit aeroplane that guided the narrator.
A false perception, one possible explanation for the mysterious plane.

sections.trick: Follow me, then no one: guided in, guided down, vanished at the runway; radar denies the rescue ever happened.
sections.examPointer: The question 'Who do you think helped the narrator?' is a classic 3 to 5 marker; offer both a rational and a mysterious explanation for good marks.

sections.heading: Characters of Both Stories
sections.para: Both stories are built around a flyer and a helper. The young seagull is timid and hesitant, yet obedient to hunger and family; he is not lazy but genuinely afraid, and his triumph is rewarding because it is earned. The mother seagull is wise and patient, understanding that threats fail where temptation succeeds, and she halts just out of reach at the crucial moment. The father and siblings appear harsh, yet their taunting also presses the young bird towards independence. In the second story the narrator is an experienced but overconfident pilot whose dream of home makes him risk the storm; in danger he is resourceful and disciplined, and honest enough to admit his fear. The mysterious pilot is silent, efficient and selfless, guiding without speaking, while the calm woman at the control room deepens the mystery with her flat denial.
points: The young seagull: timid, starving, but capable of joy once courage arrives.
The mother seagull: clever temptress, halting with the fish just beyond his beak.
The father and siblings: harsh but functional, pressing the young bird to fly.
The Dakota pilot: dreamy, risk-taking, yet skilled and composed in crisis.
The black aeroplane's pilot: wordless saviour, present exactly when needed, gone at the end.
The control room woman: matter-of-fact, her denial of any other plane seals the mystery.

keyTerms.meaning: Lacking courage, easily frightened.
Able to find ways out of difficulty.
Helping without any reward, like the mysterious pilot.
Too sure of oneself, as the pilot was before entering the storm.

sections.trick: Two helpers, two styles: the mother tempts with fish, the phantom pilot guides with a wave; both rescue without scolding.
sections.examPointer: Character sketches of the young seagull and of the Dakota pilot are common 5 markers; contrast fear conquered with risk taken.

sections.heading: Themes and Message of the Pair
sections.para: Placed together, the two stories make one lesson ring twice. 'His First Flight' says that fear is conquered by taking the first step, and that courage lies latent in every creature until necessity calls it out. 'The Black Aeroplane' says that in moments of utter helplessness, help arrives in forms we cannot explain, and that faith in such help keeps a person acting calmly until safety is reached. Both stories praise calm action over panic: the seagull does not think his way into flying, he acts; the pilot does not abandon his plane, he follows instructions and flies on. Both also reward readers with the joy of survival, the seagull floating on the green sea, the pilot safe on the runway. The combined message is that life's storms are crossed by courage, obedience to one's instincts or training, and quiet trust that help exists.
points: Fear is natural but must be faced; the first step dissolves it.
Necessity and encouragement together bring out hidden courage.
Help can come from unexpected sources in moments of crisis.
Calm action and presence of mind save lives where panic kills.
Faith, in oneself or in mysterious helpers, keeps a person going.
Both stories end in triumph, turning terror into joy and gratitude.

keyTerms.meaning: Hidden and undeveloped, like courage waiting to appear.
Quick, calm thinking in danger.
Trust in oneself or in unseen help.
A great victory, here over fear and over the storm.

sections.trick: PAIR it up: Person Acts In Reach of courage, Plane Awaits Its rescuer; both survive because both keep flying.
sections.examPointer: Comparative questions ask what the two stories teach together; answer with courage in the first and faith or help in the second.

sections.heading: Language, Devices and Quotations
sections.para: Both stories use vivid physical detail to create fear and relief. O'Flaherty paints the drop with the phrase 'the great expanse of sea stretched down beneath, and it was such a long way down, miles down', making height felt in the reader's stomach. The simile of the seagull's brothers 'curveting and banking and soaring and diving' uses rhythmic verbs to suggest grace and skill. In the second story the storm clouds are 'huge mountains of clouds', a metaphor that turns weather into landscape, and the comparison of following the stranger 'like an obedient child' shows the pilot's surrender to hope. Memorable quotations include 'his wings would never support him', 'he was afraid to fly', 'Follow me' and 'no other aeroplane was seen on the radar'. These lines serve as anchors for extract-based answers in the board examination.
points: Hyperbolic and sensory description makes the height and darkness felt: 'miles down', everything black.
Metaphor: the storm clouds are 'huge mountains of clouds'.
Simile: the narrator follows the stranger 'like an obedient child'.
Rhythmic verbs of flight, curveting, banking, soaring, diving, create grace and motion.
The contrast of joy and fear structures both stories, from taunts to triumph, from storm to runway.
Key quotations to memorise: 'his wings would never support him', 'Follow me', 'no other aeroplane on the radar'.

keyTerms.meaning: A direct comparison, like storm clouds called mountains.
A comparison using like or as, as in obedient like a child.
Tension about what happens next, built by the failed instruments.
The unexpected twist that the saviour never existed on radar.

sections.trick: MILES down, MOUNTAINS of clouds: O'Flaherty measures fear in miles, Forsyth in mountains.
sections.examPointer: Extracts are often taken from the 'miles down' passage and from the instrument-failure passage; practise explaining the effect of each image.

mcqs.question: How many of the young seagull's family members had already flown away before him?
mcqs.explanation: His two brothers and his sister had already flown away the day before, leaving the young seagull alone on his ledge.

mcqs.question: Why was the young seagull afraid to fly?
options: He felt certain his wings would never support him
His parents forbade him to fly
mcqs.explanation: Despite wings as long as his family's, he felt certain that they would never support him when he tried to fly.

mcqs.question: What trick did the mother seagull use to make her young one fly?
options: She pushed him off the ledge
She flew across with a piece of fish just out of his reach
She called other seagulls to help
She built a nest below the ledge
mcqs.explanation: She flew across to him with a piece of fish, halted just out of reach, and his dive at the fish became his first flight.

mcqs.question: What happened the moment the young seagull dived at the fish?
options: He caught the fish and stayed on the ledge
He fell into the water and drowned
His wings spread outwards and he realised he was flying
His mother caught him in her beak
mcqs.explanation: As he swooped after the fish, his wings spread outwards, the wind rushed against them, and he found himself flying.

mcqs.question: Where did the young seagull finally land after his first flight?
mcqs.explanation: He landed on the green sea, where his legs sank into the water and his belly touched it, but he floated safely.

mcqs.question: How did the young seagull's family treat his refusal to fly?
options: They taunted and threatened to let him starve on his ledge
They brought him fish every day
mcqs.explanation: His parents came around calling to him shrilly, upbraiding him and threatening to let him starve unless he flew away.

mcqs.question: Read the extract: 'His father and mother had come around calling to him shrilly, upbraiding him, threatening to let him starve on his ledge unless he flew away.' What does 'upbraiding' mean here?
mcqs.explanation: To upbraid means to scold or reproach; the parents scolded the young seagull harshly to force him out of his fear.

mcqs.question: Read the extract: 'He felt certain that his wings would never support him.' Which literary device best describes the impact of this line in the story?
options: It shows the power of fear over reason
It shows that the seagull was physically weak
It proves the parents were cruel
It indicates the seagull was ill
mcqs.explanation: The line reveals that fear, not physical weakness, held the seagull back; his certainty was an illusion born of terror.

mcqs.question: In 'The Black Aeroplane', which aeroplane was the narrator flying?
mcqs.explanation: The narrator was flying his old Dakota aeroplane, DS 088, from Paris to England.

mcqs.question: Why did the narrator of 'The Black Aeroplane' want to reach England quickly?
options: To have breakfast with his family
mcqs.explanation: He was longing to be home and dreamed of the holiday ahead and of a big English breakfast with his family.

mcqs.question: What instruction did the Paris control room give the narrator?
mcqs.explanation: Paris control instructed him to turn twelve degrees west, and he was about one hundred and fifty kilometres from Paris.

mcqs.question: Read the extract: 'The compass and the other instruments stopped working. The radio, too, was dead.' What does this moment signal in the story?
options: The peak of danger when the pilot loses all guidance
mcqs.explanation: The failure of compass, instruments and radio marks the crisis of the story: the pilot is blind in the storm with little fuel left.

mcqs.question: How much fuel did the narrator believe was left when he was inside the storm?
options: Enough for five to ten minutes
mcqs.explanation: With his tanks nearly empty, the narrator calculated that he had enough fuel for only five or ten minutes more of flying.

mcqs.question: Read the extract: 'Another aeroplane, without lights, yet strangely there, and its pilot waving, mouthing: Follow me.' Who was this pilot according to the control room woman?
options: No aeroplane was seen on the radar at all
mcqs.explanation: After the safe landing, the woman in the control centre calmly said that no other aeroplane was seen on the radar that night.

mcqs.question: What possible explanations can be offered for the mysterious black aeroplane?
options: Only a hallucination of the pilot
Only a supernatural or guardian force
A hallucination, a supernatural helper, or some unexplained rescue whose truth is never revealed
mcqs.explanation: The story deliberately leaves the rescue unexplained; readers may think of hallucination, supernatural help or an unknown saviour.

mcqs.question: What single quality does the pair of stories celebrate most?
options: Courage that overcomes fear and crisis
mcqs.explanation: Both stories show a flyer in crisis whose fear is overcome by action and trust, celebrating courage in nature and in the sky.

boardQuestions.question: Which aeroplane was the narrator flying in 'The Black Aeroplane' and where was he going?
boardQuestions.answer: The narrator was flying his old Dakota aeroplane DS 088 from Paris to England. He was eager to get home to spend the holiday with his family and to enjoy a big English breakfast with them, which is why he decided to fly through the storm rather than return to Paris.

boardQuestions.question: Why was the young seagull afraid to fly? How did his family react to his fear?
boardQuestions.answer: The young seagull was afraid because he felt certain that his wings would never support him; the great expanse of sea stretched down miles below his ledge, and the drop terrified him though his wings were as long as his family's. His parents had taught his two brothers and his sister to skim the waves and dive for fish, but he remained alone on the ledge, running back to his little hole under it. His family reacted harshly: his father and mother came around calling to him shrilly, upbraiding him and threatening to let him starve on his ledge unless he flew away, while his brothers and sister enjoyed their food in his sight. Yet no taunt could move him, for his fear was stronger than his hunger.

boardQuestions.question: How did the mother seagull tempt the young one to make his first flight? What does her trick teach us?
boardQuestions.answer: The mother seagull understood that scolding had failed, so she used temptation. She took a piece of fish and flew across to him with it, coming almost within the reach of his beak; the hungry young bird, surprised and joyful, dived at the fish with a loud scream. At the crucial moment she flew upward and halted just out of reach, so that his dive carried him outward into space. As he fell, his wings spread outwards, the wind rushed against them, and he was flying. Her trick teaches that encouragement and clever challenge work better than threats, and that courage often awakens only when necessity forces a person to act.

boardQuestions.question: Describe the young seagull's first flight in your own words. How did his feelings change during it?
boardQuestions.answer: The young seagull's first flight begins in hunger and ends in joy. Starving for twenty-four hours while his family flew and fed, he saw his mother approaching with a piece of fish and could not resist diving at it. The moment she halted just out of reach, his own momentum carried him off the ledge, and he fell outward and downward into space, terrified, his wings refusing to obey. Then instinct took over: his wings spread outwards, the wind rushed against his breast feathers and under his stomach, and the next moment he was soaring upwards instead of falling. His terror dissolved into delight; he called happily to his mother, and his brothers and sister came flying around him, curveting, banking, soaring and diving in celebration. He flew out over the green sea he had feared so much, swooped low, and finally landed on its surface, where his legs sank into the water and, when his belly touched it, he was momentarily too frightened to fly; but he floated safely, for his body was made for the sea as well as the sky. The journey of his feelings runs from doubt to panic, from panic to instinctive action, and from action to the proud joy of mastery, teaching that the first step, once taken, turns fear into freedom.

boardQuestions.question: 'Fear has to be faced to be conquered.' How does 'His First Flight' prove this statement?
boardQuestions.answer: O'Flaherty's story is a perfect illustration of the truth that fear dissolves only when it is faced. The young seagull's wings were ready; they were as long as those of his brothers and sister, yet he stood starving on his ledge because he was certain they would never support him. His fear fed on itself: the longer he looked down at the miles of empty air, the stronger his conviction of helplessness grew, and no amount of parental scolding could cure it. The cure came only through action. When hunger and his mother's tempting fish forced him to dive, he left the ledge, and at the very instant of danger his wings spread outwards and did their work. The fear that had ruled him for a whole day vanished in a single second of flight, and he was soon soaring, diving and floating on the green sea with the joy of a free bird. The story proves that fear is largely an illusion of inaction: the drop that seemed fatal became the very path to safety once it was entered. For students, the message is practical: hesitate before an examination, a speech or a new task, and the fear grows; take the first step, and the wings of ability, always present, begin to work.

boardQuestions.question: Who do you think helped the narrator of 'The Black Aeroplane'? Was it a mystery or a miracle? Justify your answer.
boardQuestions.answer: The rescue in 'The Black Aeroplane' is left deliberately unexplained, and both a mystery and a miracle can be argued. The mystery reading is rational: a pilot alone in the dark, panicking, with failed instruments, may have imagined the black aeroplane, and the simple act of following what he believed was another plane kept him flying steadily, lowering him until he broke out of the cloud and found the runway himself. The miracle reading is spiritual: help appeared exactly when fuel and hope were nearly exhausted, guided him without a single spoken word and vanished the moment safety was reached, while the radar denied that any other aircraft existed in the sky that night. Many readers therefore see the stranger as a guardian angel or an unknown benefactor whose identity the pilot, and we, can never know. What is certain is the moral either way: in moments of total helplessness a person must keep acting calmly, follow guidance when it comes and trust that help exists even when it cannot be explained. The narrator's obedience, like an obedient child, saved his life; his gratitude, searching the empty sky for his rescuer, reminds us to be thankful for unseen hands that carry us through our own storms.

boardQuestions.question: Read the extract and answer the questions: Inside the clouds, everything was suddenly black. It was impossible to see anything outside the aeroplane. The old aeroplane jumped and twisted in the air. Then the compass and the other instruments stopped working. (a) Why did the narrator enter the clouds although they were dangerous? (b) What problems did he face inside them? (c) How does the writer create suspense here?
boardQuestions.answer: 1) (a) The narrator entered the clouds because he was flying home to England and dreamed of a big breakfast with his family; although Paris control had told him to turn twelve degrees west, he decided to go through the huge storm clouds instead of returning to Paris. 2) (b) Inside the clouds he faced total darkness, for nothing could be seen outside the aeroplane windows; the old plane jumped and twisted in the air; then the compass and all other instruments stopped working, the radio went dead, and he had fuel for only five or ten minutes more. 3) (c) The writer creates suspense by stripping the pilot of every sense and support one by one: first sight, then direction, then communication, then fuel, so that each sentence deepens the reader's feeling of helplessness. 4) The blackness and the twisting motion make the danger physical, while the exact minutes of fuel place a ticking clock in the scene. 5) This suspense prepares the reader for the wonder of the mysterious black aeroplane that suddenly appears to help.

boardQuestions.question: What values do 'His First Flight' and 'The Black Aeroplane' teach us for overcoming difficulties in life?
boardQuestions.answer: Together the two stories teach a compact set of life values. From the young seagull we learn that fear is an illusion of inaction, that the first step must be taken despite trembling, and that encouragement and necessity can awaken courage which scolding never will. From the Dakota pilot we learn presence of mind in crisis, the discipline of following guidance when instruments fail, and trust in help that arrives unexpectedly. Both stories reward calm action over panic: the bird acts on instinct, the pilot acts on faith, and both survive. They also teach gratitude, for the seagull rejoices with his family and the pilot searches the sky to thank his rescuer. Finally, they remind us that every crisis, whether a ledge or a storm, is also a doorway: crossing it turns the timid creature into a flier and the lost pilot into a survivor.
